findings.title: Delete-by-time and delete-by-count run outside a single transaction, no longer atomic with tag cleanup
findings.body: CleanAnnotations now issues separate fetchIDs + deleteByIDs calls, each opening its own WithDbSession/transaction instead of sharing one transaction as before. If the process crashes or an error occurs between fetching IDs and deleting, or between deleting annotations and deleting their tags elsewhere, orphaned annotation_tag rows or partially-cleaned state can result. The PR acknowledges under-deletion but doesn't address the broader loss of atomicity between fetch and delete across concurrent writers (an annotation could be deleted concurrently with the DELETE WHERE id IN (...) still succeeding harmlessly, but a concurrently inserted/updated annotation matching the IDs is a non-issue; however, loss of the single-transaction guarantee for correctness during errors/crashes should be called out and tested).

findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
findings.body: The ticker driving srv.clean (which runs all cleanup jobs, not just annotations) was changed from every 10 minutes to every 1 minute. This is a 10x increase in frequency for all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, short URLs, query history, etc.), which seems unrelated to the stated purpose of fixing MySQL deadlocks in annotation cleanup, and may increase load/contention on the database rather than reduce it. This change is not mentioned in the PR description and could have broad unintended performance/concurrency consequences across all cleanup jobs.

findings.title: Raw ID interpolation into SQL for SQLite batch delete
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with batch size over 999, IDs are formatted directly into the SQL string via fmt.Sprint/fmt.Sprintf instead of using parameter binding. Although IDs are int64 values fetched from the DB (low injection risk here), this pattern deviates from safe parameterized queries used elsewhere and could become a problem if the code is later reused with less-trusted ID sources upon refactor.
